short: A holding action in a coastal pass that became the West's model of defiant defeat.
full:
In August or September 480 BCE a Greek force under the Spartan king Leonidas held the narrow coastal pass at Thermopylae against the invading army of Xerxes I. The ground negated Persian numbers, and for two days the Greeks held it. A local man, Ephialtes, then showed the Persians a mountain path around the pass. Leonidas dismissed most of his allies and stayed with roughly 300 Spartans, 700 Thespians and 400 Thebans; all but the Thebans were killed.

The delay bought little time. Attica was overrun and Athens burned. But the stand was mythologised at once - Simonides' epitaph, "Go tell the Spartans", was cut into stone at the pass - and it hardened Greek resolve before the naval victory at Salamis weeks later and the decisive land victory at Plataea in 479 BCE. Herodotus made it the centrepiece of his account of the Persian Wars, and it has been retold as the emblem of disciplined resistance ever since. Sabaton's "Sparta", from The Last Stand (2016), tells it from the Spartan side.
